topic: Sunk cost: how long until a local LLM rig pays for itself?

key_points: Interactive break-even calculator: pick machine, model, tokens/day, context, electricity price; returns months-to-payback plus a shareable card. This page is the direct trigger for the topic — 'Show HN: Sunk Cost' hit 47 points / 99 comments (HN item 49706656).
Models payback against a like-for-like hosted API price, and lets you toggle 'assume API prices keep falling' with a user-set rate — the only competitor that treats falling API prices as first-class.
Tracks token throughput as memory bandwidth / bytes read per token, and labels estimated (not measured) speeds explicitly.

Sub-pages worth mirroring for internal links: /best/ (quickest payback per capability class), /leaderboard/ (48 open models scored on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3 vs hosted), /how-much-memory/ (weights + KV cache arithmetic).

Its own 'best buy' headline is brutal and quotable: at 1M tokens/day, the quickest Sonnet-class payback is Qwen3.8 27B on a Mac mini M6, 32GB in 8.3 years; at 50k tokens/day the leader pays back in 166 years.
Four hardware tiers (consumer GPU, prosumer workstation, DGX Spark, multi-GPU server) x three cloud cost classes x five utilisation profiles.
Headline findings: 7B-class at 30% utilisation breaks even in 4-9 months; 70B-class on DGX Spark vs frontier APIs in 3-6 months; under 10% utilisation the horizon stretches to 2-4 years.
Power and cooling add 15-25% on top of hardware TCO at US rates, more in Europe.

Hardware TCO table (3-year amortisation, 24/7 power at $0.15/kWh): RTX 5090 build $3,500 upfront -> $5,120 3-yr TCO; Mac Studio M5 Max 128GB $3,499 -> $4,429; DGX Spark $3,000 -> $6,150; 2x H100 server $60,000 -> $78,900.
Explicitly concedes the arbitrage has compressed in 2026 as inference prices fell, and that local only wins decisively on data-residency-sensitive workloads.
Scenario framing that matches how readers self-select: casual (150k tok/mo), developer (3M tok/mo), power user (15M tok/mo), enterprise team (20 devs, 60M tok/mo).

Hardware table with effective monthly cost amortised over 3 years: RTX 4060 8GB PC $37-43/mo; RTX 4090 24GB PC $80-95/mo; Mac mini M4 16GB $19/mo; Mac mini M4 Pro 48GB $60/mo; Mac Studio M4 Max 128GB $117/mo.
Verdict per tier: cloud wins for casual use; near break-even for medium; local wins by $100-200/mo with 3-8 month payback at heavy use.
Assumes $0.12/kWh and 4 hours/day average use — a soft electricity assumption the post can correct upward.
Full 12- and 36-month TCO model across light (<1M tok/day), medium (1-10M tok/day) and heavy (10M-100M+ tok/day) tiers; aims at solo devs, startups and mid-size teams.
Names the costs everyone underestimates: electricity, cooling, ops labour, hardware depreciation, rate-limit engineering, and re-engineering prompts when a vendor changes models.
Claims 2026 break-even points are ~40% lower than 2024 — useful counter-claim to test against per-token numbers.
Weakness to attack: its pricing note admits hardware MSRPs and API rates date to mid-2025, so its own totals are stale a year on.
Blends a per-month local cost into a single break-even threshold: RTX 4090 ~$104/mo all-in beats GPT-4o at ~8M tok/mo but needs 204M+ tok/mo to beat GPT-4o-mini.
Worked Llama 3 70B Q4 on RTX 4090 example: ~$130/mo all-in, ~$1.11 per 1M tokens at full utilisation.
States the dirty secret plainly: at moderate volume the cheapest managed open-weight APIs are often cheaper than local hosting; local wins decisively only at 500M+ tok/mo, or when privacy dominates.
Retrieved via search snippet only — direct fetch returned HTTP 403 (Cloudflare). Do not cite the page as if it had been read.

stats.fact: US average residential electricity price was 18.34 c/kWh as of June 2026, up from 15.04 c/kWh in 2022 (+22% in four years), with EIA forecasting a further 3-5%/year through 2027; state range runs from 13.11c (Nevada, June 2026) to 52.72c (Hawaii).
stats.source: EIA Electric Power Monthly Table 5.6.A, as reported by priceofelectricity.com and electricityrateperkwh.com (both June 2026); gerahome.com cites the April 2026 figure at 18.83 c/kWh

stats.fact: Most local-vs-cloud analyses still assume $0.12-$0.15/kWh (for example llmconfigurator.com uses $0.12, presenc.ai uses $0.15), which understates power cost by roughly 20-50% against the current US residential average.
stats.source: llmconfigurator.com local-vs-cloud guide; presenc.ai local LLM vs cloud API cost report

stats.fact: A representative 2026 hardware amortisation set: RTX 5090 desktop build ~$3,500 upfront / ~$1,707 per year; Mac Studio M5 Max 128GB ~$3,499 / ~$1,476 per year; NVIDIA DGX Spark ~$3,000 / ~$2,050 per year; dual-H100 server ~$60,000 / ~$26,300 per year.
stats.source: presenc.ai, Local LLM vs Cloud API Cost Comparison 2026 (3-year amortisation)

stats.fact: DGX Spark vs Mac Studio M5 Max at 70B Q4: power cost per 1M output tokens ~$0.60 (Spark, 600-800W under inference) vs ~$0.25 (M5 Max, 150-200W) at $0.15/kWh; total amortised cost per 1M tokens lands within 3% of each other (~$1.70 vs ~$1.75) because Apple's higher hardware amortisation cancels its power advantage.
stats.source: presenc.ai, NVIDIA DGX Spark vs Mac Studio M5 Max for Local AI 2026

stats.fact: Throughput gap on one generation: GeForce RTX 5090 hits 205.5 decode tok/s vs DGX Spark at 60.9 tok/s (3.4x), with prefill 8,518.6 vs 2,054.0 tok/s on the same benchmark.
stats.source: AIMultiple, DGX Spark inference benchmarks (via presenc.ai and aimultiple.com/dgx-spark-alternatives)

stats.fact: Worked example from our own model: a $3,500 RTX 5090 rig at 205 tok/s, 20h/day, at $0.183/kWh produces ~443M tokens/month at ~$163/month all-in. Against a hosted open-weight model at ~$0.50/M output that is ~$886/month of API, so payback is ~4.8 months; against ~$0.08/M it never pays back.
stats.source: Calculated for this brief from presenc.ai hardware TCO, EIA electricity price and OpenRouter live pricing (2026-09-29)

stats.fact: Same rig, same assumptions, held at 24/7 utilisation and compared against ~$0.50/M output: payback stretches to ~39 months. At 12h/day it never pays back, because the API bill ($133/mo) is under the local cost ($137/mo).
stats.source: Calculated for this brief (see stats above for inputs)

stats.fact: A 32GB Radeon R9700 at $1,350 replaced a $300+/month GitHub Copilot bill for one HN commenter, who reports a ~4-month payoff — and that is the optimistic end of community reports.
stats.source: Hacker News comment thread on Sunk Cost (item 49706656)

stats.fact: At 1M tokens/day the quickest Sonnet-class local payback on Sunk Cost's own model is 8.3 years (Qwen3.8 27B on a Mac mini M6 32GB at an estimated 6.9 tok/s); only at agent-scale ~20M tokens/day does it drop under a year. A 50k tokens/day user pays back in 166 years.
stats.source: sunkcost.ai/best/ and the author's reply in the HN thread (item 49706656)

stats.fact: OpenRouter live pricing on 2026-09-29: cheapest per-token endpoints run $0.02-$0.10/M output (mistral-nemo $0.030, gpt-oss-20b $0.090, llama-3.1-8b $0.080, gemma-3-4b $0.100), while frontier hosts sit at $10-$75/M output (claude-opus-5 $25, claude-fable-5.1 $50, gpt-6-astra $50, claude-opus-4.1 $75).

The capability gap does not close with hardware: the best open-weight model on Sunk Cost's board scores 42 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3 (GLM-5.3-Flash, 189GB of weights) against 53 for the best hosted model — an 11-point gap.

Memory is two numbers held at once. Llama 3.3 70B Instruct at Q4_K_M needs 42.5GB of weights plus 10.7GB of KV cache at 32k context = 53.3GB, because the cache is 327,680 bytes per token across 80 layers — the window you ask for is a hardware purchase decision, not a setting.

Community counter-evidence on hardware price inflation: used RTX 3090s were bought for ~$500 each post-merge, one commenter runs Qwen 3.8 at 57 tok/s on a $2,000 used HP Omen with a 3090, and another reports hardware value doubling or tripling since purchase.
stats.source: Hacker News thread on Sunk Cost (item 49706656)

angles: Write the how-to as a five-number worksheet, not a verdict: throughput (tok/s) x hours/day = tokens/month; electricity (W x h x your kWh rate); amortisation period you actually believe; the API tier you are really replacing; and what else the idle hours do. Most payback arguments fail because people compare a GPU at 100% utilisation against an API bill from a month when they barely used it.

The utilisation cliff is the real answer. Same $3,500 rig: payback ~4.8 months at 20h/day against a $2/M tier, ~39 months at 24/7 against $0.50/M, and never at 12h/day. Payback is not a property of the machine, it is a property of your queue depth.

Publish the breakeven against the correct comparator, then show it is usually the wrong one. Local mid-tier models (~$0.50-1.25/M hosted) are what you are actually replacing on capability; against frontier pricing the same rig 'pays back' in a month or two and that number is a category error.

Counter the falling-price assumption with live 2026 data: cheapest hosted open-weight output is already $0.03-$0.10/M. Any model with a flat API price predicts a payback that repricing can erase — so include an 'API prices fall X%/year' line, the way Sunk Cost does.

Correct the electricity assumption upward with EIA data: most write-ups still use $0.12-$0.15/kWh while the US residential average was 18.34c in June 2026 and is forecast to rise 3-5%/year. At $0.40/kWh a 600W rig under load can push payback past the depreciation window entirely.
Include the idle-power asymmetry: DGX Spark draws ~120W idle vs ~25W for a Mac Studio, which is why a lower-upfront box can lose on TCO once you count the hours it is plugged in and not generating.

Reframe the honest answer as three separate ledgers: money (often never pays back at hobby volume), capability (an 11-point gap that hardware cannot close), and control/autonomy (what the HN thread's top commenters actually bought and what no calculator can price). Say plainly which ledger the reader is asking about.

Show the agent-workload exception with real numbers: 24/7 batch and subagent generation is the one regime where a local rig wins on cash alone, because the bottleneck is queue time, not token price — while noting that a Max/Pro plan can serve more concurrency than a single-GPU rig.

Give a concrete decision rule with thresholds instead of vibes, for example: under ~50M tokens/month on a cheap hosted model, stay on the API; 50-500M/month, buy only if you already need the hardware or the data cannot leave; 500M+/month sustained, local wins on cash.

Close with the sunk cost trap itself: once the box is bought, the marginal token is nearly free and the API comparison becomes a way to justify a machine you wanted anyway. Name that honestly and give the reader a pre-purchase test they can run in a spreadsheet.
